slides: Open by locating the chapter after the invariance story. Chapter 3 made the probability simplex feel rigid; Chapter 4 relaxes normalization by moving to positive measures. The lecture should repeatedly ask what becomes flat in the larger cone and what bends again when probabilities are renormalized.

Use this route slide as a map of dialects. Alpha coordinates, Tsallis q entropy, escort distributions, expert pooling, and log-det matrix divergence can sound unrelated. The chapter's real lesson is that each one is a representation choice plus a checkable invariant.

Stress the distinction between positive measures and probabilities. The power coordinate h alpha straightens the cone because every component can scale freely. The probability simplex imposes a sum constraint, so the same straight line in representation space usually returns as a curved path after normalization.

Treat the geodesic picture as a laboratory readout. The endpoints are fixed, but changing alpha changes which coordinate system sees a straight segment. Students should inspect where the curve bends toward the boundary and remember that the bend is caused by normalization, not by a failure of flatness upstairs.

Make the divergence slide computational rather than ceremonial. At alpha equal zero, the square-root coordinate turns the local geometry into a Euclidean comparison, so the Pythagorean check becomes visible. The broader alpha family keeps the same habit: choose coordinates, project there, and verify the residual.

Connect q and alpha immediately so students do not treat Tsallis entropy as a separate topic. The relation alpha equals two q minus one tells them that deformed logarithms are another notation for a power-coordinate geometry. The entropy curves show how boundary emphasis changes with q.

Use escorts as a concrete reweighting experiment. For q greater than one, large coordinates become even more visible; for q less than one, small coordinates gain relative weight. The geometric point is that this is a coordinate system, not merely a heuristic smoothing trick.

Frame alpha integration as an applied version of the chapter's main move. Each expert distribution is lifted into h alpha coordinates, averaged linearly, and normalized back. The choice of alpha controls whether pooling behaves mixture-like, multiplicative, or somewhere between those endpoints.

Move carefully from diagonal positive measures to full positive-definite matrices. Eigenvalues behave like positive masses, but orientations now matter too. The Stein or log-det divergence is useful because it respects congruence transformations, the matrix analogue of changing coordinates without changing the geometry.

Use the landscape slide to make nonnegativity and boundary behavior inspectable. Around the identity, the log-det divergence has a clear minimum. Near loss of positive definiteness the surface steepens sharply, reminding students that the positive cone has a real boundary even when formulas look smooth.

The synthesis slide should name the three recurring choices: representation, normalization, and invariant test. Positive measures are flat in alpha coordinates, probabilities bend after normalization, escorts reweight coordinates, and SPD matrices demand congruence-invariant matrix formulas. These are variations on one organizing habit.

Close with a short diagnostic activity. Ask students to identify the representation, the constraint, and the invariant for a proposed calculation. If they can answer those three questions for alpha geodesics, Tsallis entropy, escorts, and log-det divergence, the chapter's many objects become one coherent toolkit.
